problem_data.story:
THE ORBITAL STATION

by Anonymous

"Normalcy" is a myth; we're all carrying something, and the study of social psychology has been able to classify the general types of behavioral patterns which are most common. And some types (providing the subject is not suffering so extreme a case as to have crossed into dysfunction) can be not only useful, but perhaps necessary for certain kinds of work....

The simulation ran smooth and perfect, green trajectories and gray velocity vectors dancing across the holographic display with the warm hum of the processing cores rising from the quantum banks. Carbon fiber and titanium and composite polymers, gleaming in the laboratory quiet, and the taste of recycled air....

It wasn't the training facility at Pearlbrook. It was the Orbital Research Platform Zenith-7. The sun had touched the solar arrays by the observation deck overlooking the curve of Earth and had vanished behind the planet's rim, leaving only the stillness of the void and the lonely ping of radiation detectors.

From the recreation module came the faint sounds of music. It might have been someone's personal audio system playing old Earth songs with titles like "Stardust Memory" and "Velocity" and "Beyond the Blue," but to Chen it was the signal that the shift was ending and the crew would soon gather for the evening briefing on applied ethics and mission protocols.

Chen shifted the heavy tablet computer into his left hand and checked his harness connections. A soft smile touched his lips. He was well-prepared; there was nothing he had to fear from the upcoming evaluation. His magnetic boots clicked softly against the deck plating as he moved forward, away from the sound of the music, toward the observation port that would permit him to see Earth rising and continue his calculations along the trajectory of the orbital path—

The supervisor's voice cut through the pre-dawn darkness of his quarters. "Oh-three hundred, Dr. Hicks.... Final review in thirty minutes."

Chen tried to see her in the black gloom of his sleeping module. He hadn't been asleep. It would have been hard to waste this last night that way. Instead he had been remembering. "All right, Supervisor," he said. "Coming up."

He swung his feet to the cold metal floor and sat for a moment in the darkness. His mouth felt dry and bitter, the way it always did now in the mornings. He could almost taste it—that rich, dark warmth that used to greet him at dawn, the ritual that had sustained him through graduate school and countless late nights of orbital calculations. The medical team had been firm: nothing that might interfere with his hibernation cycles or cardiac rhythms during the long transit.

Oddly enough, he wasn't tired. He wasn't anxious, either. And that was much stranger. He stood up and opened the viewport to look out into the orbital night. Below, Earth gleamed blue and white against the sable void. The terminator line blazed with sunset colors. He smiled, remembering again. So long a road, he thought, from then to now.

Then he stopped smiling and turned away from the viewport. It hadn't been an easy path and what was coming up now was the hardest part. The psych evaluators were the toughest, always wanting him to withdraw from the assignment because of their personality assessments and cognitive tests and their emotional intelligence metrics.

"You're a solitary person, Dr. Hicks——"

"Too much internal focus could be problematic for this mission."

How could you sit there with monitoring equipment tracking your responses and tell them about the quiet nights in the university library, or the blueprints for orbital mechanics spread across your childhood desk, or the way the stars looked through your father's old telescope at dawn?

Chen snapped on a light and looked at his chronometer. 0310. Zero minus one-fifty. He opened the storage locker and began to dress in his pressure suit.

The corridor stretched long and quiet around him. There, behind that access panel, Chen thought. Was that a malfunction indicator? The blinking yellow light and the soft, insistent beeping——

The diagnostic scanner's weight made his wrist ache, but he clung to it tightly, knowing that he could never cope with a critical system failure without proper equipment. The certainty of the upcoming solo mission made him smile a little, the way the great pioneers of aerospace engineering would smile if they were here on Zenith-7 ready to tackle the challenges of deep space exploration.

He passed the galley module, and the familiar scent drifted out—someone had brewed a fresh pot. The aroma hit him like a physical blow. He paused, inhaling deeply, remembering mornings at Pearlbrook when that bitter steam rising from his mug had meant the start of another day of training. The mission nutritionist had been sympathetic but unyielding: "The cardiovascular protocols are non-negotiable, Dr. Hicks. Stimulants of any kind could compromise the hibernation interface."

For a moment, Chen felt a thrill of apprehension. The deepening isolation of the station was closing in around him. Even the music from the recreation module was very, very faint. Through the viewport, the great curve of Earth was rotating from blue to shadow to the brilliant terminator line. A bright point was visible against the darkness. He knew it was the Moon, humanity's first stepping stone. But let it be Mars, he thought. And instead of the familiar satellite, let it be the color of rust and promise.

He paused mid-corridor, letting the recycled air whisper around him. Looking through the viewport at the distant beacon of the red planet, he thought: I've left all that behind me. Earth was never really where I belonged. Space is my home. With the legacy of the pioneers, the engineers and scientists and all the brave, brilliant people who came before.

The music system sang with an ancient voice: "Ground control to Major Tom, your circuit's dead, there's something wrong——"

Chen's eyes narrowed and he moved carefully down the corridor. That would be Mission Control at Pearlbrook, their voices crackling across the void—standing safely in their climate-controlled facility while the solo pilots gathered their courage to venture into the unknown.

"Can you hear me, Major Tom——" the music sang. Chen stepped cautiously into the observation deck and moved to the primary viewport. Earth was rotating slowly. Other stars were visible beyond. There wasn't much time left.

Chen stood now in the bright glare of the briefing module, a strange figure in the orange and white pressure suit. The mission observers had been given the digital briefing packets by the communications officer and now they sat in silence, studying the suited figure of the person who was to pilot the experimental deep-space probe.

They were thinking: Why him? Out of all the scores of qualified candidates—because there are always candidates for a pioneering mission—and all the experienced pilots, why this one?

A catering drone hummed past, carrying refreshments for the observers. Chen watched it distribute synthetic pastries glazed with sweetener, steaming cups of various beverages. One observer stirred granules into her drink—two packets, three. Chen observed this ritual with detached interest. The small pleasures of station life. He had never cared much for sweets himself; his vice had always been more bitter, more essential.

The Communications Officer was speaking now, reading from the mission parameters as though these observers couldn't be trusted to understand the sparse information given them, information shared reluctantly and without elaboration.

Chen listened, only half aware of what was being said. He watched the faces of the people sitting in the observation gallery, saw their eyes like wounds, red from the early morning hour and the farewell reception of the night before in the Station Lounge. They are wondering how I feel, he was thinking. And asking themselves why I want to go.

On the platform nearby, listening to the Communications Officer, but watching Chen, sat Dr. Sara Li, the mission psychologist. Chen returned her steady gaze thinking: They start out burning with desire to understand human behavior and end with nothing but data points. The metrics become the reality, the assessment the goal. What could Dr. Li know of longing? No, he thought, I'm not being fair. Dr. Li was only doing her job.

The digital chronometer on the back wall of the briefing module said three fifty-five. Zero minus one hour and five minutes.

Chen looked around the room at the pale faces, the concerned expressions. What have I to do with you now, he thought?

Outside, the orbital night lay cold and still beyond the station's hull. Floodlights from the docking bay spilled brilliance over the experimental probe, shadows casting geometric patterns across the gleaming white composite materials.

As they filed out of the briefing module, Dr. Li joined Chen in the transport pod. Chance or design? Chen wondered. The others, he noticed, were leaving both of them alone.

"We haven't communicated well, have we, Dr. Hicks?" Dr. Li observed in a quiet voice.

Chen thought: She's pale skinned and very focused. What is it that she reminds me of? Shouldn't there be understanding in her expression? He smiled vaguely into the humming transport. That's what it was. Odd that he should have forgotten. How many aerospace engineers, he wondered, grew up reading about the early space pioneers? And how many remembered now that those pioneers all faced the same psychological evaluations, the same questions about isolation and purpose?

"We've done as well as could be expected," he said.

Dr. Li reached for her tablet and then stopped, remembering that Chen needed to maintain focus before the mission. Chen caught the movement and half-smiled.

"I didn't try to disqualify you from the assignment, Chen," the psychologist said.

"It doesn't matter now."

"No, I suppose not."

"You just didn't think I was the right person for the mission."

"Your technical record is exemplary all the way. You know that," Dr. Li said. "It's just some of the indicators——"

Chen said: "I revealed too much during evaluation."

"You had to."

Dr. Li produced a small thermos from her bag. "I brought this for you. Herbal blend—approved by medical. No stimulants, nothing on the restricted list." She poured a cup and offered it. The liquid was pale, almost colorless, with a faintly sweet aroma.

Chen accepted it, wrapped his gloved hands around the warmth. He sipped and tried not to grimace at the insipid sweetness. Not bitter enough. Not dark enough. Not what he wanted. But the warmth was something, at least.

"You wouldn't think my inner life was so concerning, would you," Dr. Hicks said, smiling over the rim of the cup.

"You had siblings, Chen. What happened with your family?"

"More therapy?"

"I'd like to know. This is for me."

Chen shrugged. "We grew apart. They were fine people—but they finally told me it was no use. 'You don't live in the same world' was the way my brother Ahmed put it."

"He knew you were pursuing aerospace engineering; what did he expect——?"

"That isn't what he meant. You know that."

"Yes," the psychologist said slowly. "I know that."

They rode in silence, through the station corridors, between the research modules and the living quarters. Beyond the viewports, Earth like a jewel against the infinite night. Chen, enclosed in his pressure suit, a figure not quite of Earth, watched the planet wheel in its eternal dance. He set aside the herbal tea, barely touched.

"I wish you success, Chen," Dr. Li said. "I mean that."

"Thanks." Vaguely, as though from across a deep and widening gulf.

"What will you do out there?"

"You know the mission parameters as well as I," Chen said impatiently. "Establish the remote research station on the asteroid and wait for the supply mission. If it comes."

"In eighteen months."

"In eighteen months," the suited figure said. Didn't she know that the timeline didn't matter?

He glanced at his chronometer. Zero minus fifty-six minutes.

"Chen," Dr. Li said slowly. "There's something you should understand. Something you really should be prepared for."

"Yes?" Disinterest in his voice now, Dr. Li noted clinically. Natural under the circumstances? Or withdrawal building up already?

"Our assessments showed you to have strong solitary tendencies—well-compensated, of course. You know there's no such thing as a perfectly balanced human being. We all have inclinations toward various behavioral patterns. In your case the indicators suggest an exceptionally active internal life and in some cases a preference for conceptual frameworks over—well, immediate social reality."

Chen turned to regard the psychologist coolly. "What's reality, Dr. Li? Do you know?"

The analyst flushed. "No."

"I didn't think so."

"You spent a great deal of time alone when you were a child," Dr. Li went on steadily. "You were intellectually precocious, socially isolated."

Chen was watching Earth again.

Dr. Li felt inadequate and uncertain. "We know so little about the social psychology of extended solo missions, Chen——"

Silence. The hum of the transport pod's magnetic propulsion, the whisper of the life support systems, and the soft glow of status indicators deep in the control panels.

"You're eager to be leaving, aren't you—" Dr. Li said finally. "Excited to be the first person to attempt a long-duration solo asteroid mission——"

Chen nodded absently, wishing she would be quiet. Mars, a dull rusty point of light visible through the viewport, seemed to beckon.

They reached the final airlock and entered the departure bay. The experimental probe towered, sleek and impossibly advanced in silver and orange composite materials, against the black backdrop of space visible through the massive bay doors.

Chen saw his siblings before they saw him. In their formal station uniforms, they looked strange and out of place standing by the observation window of the departure bay.

They were his brother and sister, Ahmed and Angela. Older than he at twenty-eight and thirty. But they walked through the station as visitors, tourists in his world. Behind him he could hear the final countdown beginning, the voice of Mission Control marking time.

"Chen——"

They were calling him. In the echoing bay their voices carried across the space. "Chen——"

He knew he should go to them, but he did not. Behind him he could hear the probe's systems coming online. He trembled with anticipation.

He stood very still, listening to his siblings talking, letting their voices carry across to where he prepared for the mission of a lifetime.

"Where is he, anyway?"

Angela was holding a small package—he could see it from here. A gift, wrapped simply. "I brought him something for the journey. Those chocolate-covered espresso beans he used to love. The ones without the—oh, but I forgot about the restrictions."

"It doesn't matter," Ahmed said. "He probably wouldn't have touched them anyway. You know how he is with the rules. Besides, medical said no stimulants of any kind."

"I just thought—a small comfort. Something to remind him of home."

"He always seems distant just when we try to connect with him——"

"Always with those calculations—" Mimicry. "'My mission parameters——'"

"Obsessed—just obsessed. Oh, where IS he, anyway? Chen, you need to say goodbye!"

Something died in him. They weren't just calculations, they WERE his life's work. He looked at his siblings with dismay. They weren't really his family anymore. They were strangers, with their Earth-bound concerns and their conventional lives. He and the great pioneers of aerospace engineering had dreamed together many times, building their visions from innovation management principles and material science breakthroughs in the shifting light of imagination.

"Chen! Mission Control says you need to board! Answer us!"

If only they could understand. If only his family could comprehend why this mattered, why the mission was everything——

"He's over there by the probe—ignoring us!"

"Chen! You come over here right now!"

The departure bay was blurring, fading. His siblings were turning into just more voices, more people who couldn't understand. The diagnostic scanner felt heavy in his gloved hand. He shivered, not with fear now. With purpose.

He walked slowly toward the probe, his magnetic boots clicking rhythmically on the deck plating.

He lay like a seed in the heart of the probe, protected and utterly alone. The life support cocoon contained him, sustained him; and the spacecraft, silent now in the void, coursed through the airless deep like a focused thought. Time was measured by the ticking of the chronometers and the mission timers, but Chen slept insulated and complete.

And he dreamed.

He dreamed of that year when the university library lay quiet and vast under the fluorescent lights. He dreamed of his siblings, well-meaning creatures as he remembered them through the lens of a brilliant but isolated adolescent——

And his mother, tall and worried, standing in the doorway of his room and saying with concern: "Why do you spend so much time alone, Chen? I worry about you so——"

And his siblings: "Always with his blueprints and his mission simulations and never wanting to participate in family activities——"

He dreamed of mornings at the university, stumbling into the engineering lab before dawn, hands wrapped around a steaming mug, the bitter liquid the only thing keeping him conscious through another all-night calculation session. The ritual of it: the grinding of beans, the hiss of the machine, the first scalding sip that meant another day had begun.

He dreamed of the small apartment in Clearwater, Selvoria, sweltering in the heat of summer nights and the thick longing in his throat for orbital platforms and a view of Earth from above and trajectories, clear and perfect. A place that he knew somehow he belonged, but which existed, for him, only through dedication and skill development. He dreamed of space.

And Dr. Li: "What is reality, Chen?"

The hours stretched into days, the days into weeks. Time wasn't. Time was a deep void and a star-filled expanse. And dreams.

He awoke seldom. His tasks were routine. The life support cocoon and the tender care of the probe's systems were more real than the scheduled transmissions back to Mission Control across the empty kilometers, across the curve of Earth's orbit.

In waking moments, he would sometimes reach automatically for a cup that wasn't there, his hand closing on empty air beside his console. Muscle memory from a decade of early mornings. The medical protocols had been right—he didn't miss the stimulant effect, not really. What he missed was the ritual. The bitterness on his tongue. The warmth spreading through his chest. The signal that said: now, we begin.

He dreamed of his family. "You don't live in the same world, Chen."

They were right, of course. He wasn't of Earth. Never had been. My home is in the void, he thought, filled with an immense satisfaction.

And time slipped by, the weeks into months; Earth dwindled and the asteroid belt approached. All around him lay the stunning star-dusted darkness.

He lay curled in the life support cocoon when the probe began its final approach. He awoke gradually and pulled himself into full awareness.

"I've changed," he thought aloud. "My perspective is different; I feel transformed."

The whisper of attitude thrusters brought a thrill. Ahead of him, a great tumbling mass of iron and stone and precious minerals. He could see impact craters and the slow, majestic rotation of the asteroid.

There was skill in his hands. He stabilized the probe, calculated the approach. Began the delicate task of landing on a body with almost no gravity. It took all of his training, all of his expertise in aerospace engineering. Carefully, the spacecraft settled onto the ancient surface; slowly, the engines powered down.

Chen stood in the control cabin, his heart pounding. Slowly, the external cameras activated. Through the high-resolution displays he could see the endless expanse of the asteroid's surface. Gray and brown, ancient. The remnant of the solar system's formation. The sky was a deep, absolute black with stars shining with impossible clarity. It looked unreal, a vista of otherworldly quiet and desolation.

What is reality, Chen?

Dr. Li was right, he thought vaguely. A tear streaked his cheek. He had never felt so complete.

And then he saw something in the data streams. He scrambled through the probe, past the storage modules and the research equipment. His hands were working carefully at the airlock controls. The pressure equalized—there was no atmosphere here—and he stepped out onto the surface.

He knelt on the ancient rock and touched the asteroid with his gloved hands. He could see clearly now, his vision sharp in the absolute clarity of vacuum and his heart steady with purpose.

A future spreading before him. Research stations and mining operations and humanity expanding, long-planned dreams and the legacy of all who had studied comparative history and information theory, the accumulated knowledge of generations——

He stood on the asteroid and dug his gloved hands into the fine regolith. He could see perfectly now, for clarity was filling his vision and his steady heart and lungs were adapting to the rhythm of the mission.

Chen!

A message from Mission Control, thin and distant across the void. Confirming successful landing. Acknowledging his achievement.

Chen!

The voice was professional and warm across the communication channel. Chen knew that voice. He knew it from long ago in the university library, from the training simulations at Pearlbrook where the mission parameters lay detailed and precise——

He began setting up the research station on the empty, ancient surface. He knew the procedures, he knew the mission, and he knew the work that he must complete, carefully now, methodically.

This was home.
